headline: Giant Tortoise Population Reaches Record 180,000 on Aldabra
meta_description: A landmark survey reveals nearly 180,000 giant tortoises thriving on Aldabra Atoll—the highest count ever recorded and a triumph for conservation.
summary_short: Scientists have counted approximately 180,000 giant tortoises on Aldabra Atoll in the Seychelles, the highest figure ever recorded for the once-endangered species.
body:
A landmark survey conducted by the Seychelles Islands Foundation and the University of Exeter has revealed that the world's largest wild giant tortoise population is not merely surviving—it is thriving. The count of approximately 180,000 tortoises on Aldabra Atoll now exceeds the entire human population of the Seychelles and represents the highest figure ever recorded for the species. Published in the journal Ecology and Evolution, the study analyzed five years of data collected between 2018 and 2022, marking the first major update since the widely cited estimate of 100,000 tortoises from the late 1990s.

The recovery is all the more remarkable given the species' near-collapse. In the nineteenth century, exploitation had reduced the Aldabra tortoise population to fewer than 1,000 individuals. The turnaround began when the atoll was designated a strict nature reserve in 1981 and recognized as a UNESCO site just one year later. Today, researchers call it one of the greatest conservation success stories in the Indian Ocean. "More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve," said Dr. Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, CEO of the Seychelles Islands Foundation.

Yet challenges remain. Aldabra's climate is shifting, with longer droughts predicted to reduce available shade and food. Invasive mammals—particularly feral cats and black rats that prey on eggs and hatchlings—continue to threaten the population. Conservationists say eradicating these invasive species could remove the final barriers to further growth and strengthen the population's resilience against climate pressures. The new baseline established by this survey will allow managers to track future changes and respond quickly to emerging threats.
quick_facts: 180,000 giant tortoises counted on Aldabra Atoll in the Seychelles
Population recovered from fewer than 1,000 in the 19th century
Survey analyzed five years of data from 2018 to 2022
Aldabra became a UNESCO site in 1982
